artifactEvidence.excerpt: On September 1, the US Department of Justice submitted an argument supporting OpenAI in the New York copyright lawsuits. It urged the court to treat copying written work to teach AI patterns as fair use: certain uses US law permits without the copyright owner’s permission.

The filing separates three things that can get bundled into “AI used someone’s work”. A developer first obtains material. During training, software adjusts numerical settings using examples, developing patterns it can apply later. The trained part that produces a response is the model. When someone uses it, the answer it produces is an output.

explainBack.question: Why does the government argue that copying newspaper articles to train an AI can be fair use, when copying an article to republish it clearly would not be?
explainBack.answer: Because fair use is judged per use, not per act of copying. When articles are used in training, software adjusts numerical settings to extract statistical patterns of language; the purpose is building a tool that generates responses, not delivering those articles to readers. Republishing serves the same purpose as the original and substitutes for it, so the same copying gets a different legal question — just as recording a programme to watch later differs from selling the tape. And the filing itself concedes an output that reconstructs and distributes a work can raise yet another question.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: The stage separation and pattern-extraction mechanism (P005), the different-purpose argument (P006), the case-by-case factor framework (P007), and the VCR mapping with its retained limit (P008, P009).
explainBack.assessment: The article fully supports this answer: mechanism, purpose distinction, use-by-use framing and the output caveat are all present in the reader's ordinary language.
